parts: Lesson 13: Growth and Patterns of Tourism in India — Summary

An international tourist is a person visiting India on a foreign passport who stays at least 24 hours for leisure, health, study, religion, sport, business or meeting friends without taking a paid job (diplomats and armed forces do not count). A domestic tourist travels within the country to a place other than the usual residence or work and stays at least 24 hours in accommodation; people visiting their home town for social functions do not count. Tourists spend nearly 40% of their money on handicrafts such as jewellery, carpets, leather, ivory and brass work. 'Atithi Devo Bhava' (guest is God) and Nehru's 'Welcome as a tourist and send them back as a friend' show India's tradition. India's tourism is natural (mountain, island, desert, coastal, lacustrine, wildlife, adventure) and cultural (religious, historical, traditional, health, sports, rural).

Health tourism (low-cost world-class treatment; ayurveda, naturopathy, unani, siddha; tourists from the US, Europe and the Middle East), spiritual tourism (India as the confluence of religions), adventure tourism (mostly at high altitude), MICE tourism (Meetings, Incentives, Conferences and Exhibitions, fast-growing since liberalisation in 1991), rural tourism (interaction with local people and their cultural life) and sustainable tourism (meeting present needs without harming future generations; minimum impact on the environment).

Growth can be positive (more tourists) or negative (fewer). Tourism grew rapidly after the second half of the 20th century and substantially after the 1990s because of the wealth and leisure time of tourists from rich countries and better transport, communication and accommodation. South Asia's high growth in 1990: India captures more than half of South Asia's tourist arrivals and about 75% of its receipts. Two main measures of the tourism index are international tourist arrivals and tourism receipts.

Factors affecting growth: geographical (climate, landscape, location: plains tourists go to hill stations in summer), cultural events (Durga Puja, Holi, Diwali, Goa Carnival, Dandiya, Desert Festival, Surajkund Mela, Onam), safety and security (Kashmir fell after 1985 because of terrorism), economic conditions (higher incomes travel more), facilities and services (accommodation, transport, banking, guides) and government policies (subsidies, packages and a liberal visa policy).

FTAs were only 16,829 in 1951 and rose to 1.14 million in 1981 and 6.30 million in 2011; they were 23.33 million in 2015 (the 4.4% growth); 2009 had a small fall and 2001–02 and 2012 also fell. India's share in international arrivals was 0.40% in 1997 and 0.64% in 2011 (below 1%). India's world rank improved from 54th in 2002 to 38th in 2011 and 24th in 2015 (the lesson also notes 52nd in the Travel and Tourism Competitiveness Report 2015). Top ten source countries in 2014: USA 14.57%, Bangladesh 12.27%, UK 10.92%, then Sri Lanka, Russia, Canada, Malaysia, France, Australia and Germany (61.54% together). Foreign tourists stay a little over a month. State share of foreign tourist visits in 2014: Tamil Nadu 20.6% (first), Maharashtra 19.4%, Uttar Pradesh, Delhi, Rajasthan, West Bengal, Kerala, Bihar, Karnataka and Haryana (2.4%, the lowest of the top ten). In 2011 Maharashtra led with 24.7%. The most popular monuments are the Taj Mahal, Qutub Minar and Agra Fort.

Growth of domestic tourism comes from rising income, purchasing power and the dynamic middle class. Domestic tourists were 159.88 million in 1997, 526.70 million in 2007 and 1,431.97 million in 2015. Top states in 2015: Tamil Nadu (23.3%), Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal, Gujarat and Rajasthan; the top five states account for about two-thirds (63.3%) of domestic visits; the top ten for about 84–85%.

Tourism is a 'smokeless industry' with a unique ability to earn foreign exchange (which helps the balance of trade). Money spent by tourists is tourist receipt. FEEs were US$ 16.56 billion in 2011 against 14.19 billion in 2010 (16.7% growth). India's share in world tourism receipts was 0.64% in 1997 and reached 1.61% in 2011. FEEs in January–April 2013 were US$ 6.878 billion against US$ 6.145 billion a year earlier (9.61% growth). Government steps: a tourist branch in 1949, a separate Tourism Department in 1957, the Tourism Development Council in 1958, planning from the Second Five Year Plan, the National Policy on Tourism in 1982, industry status in the Seventh Plan (1985–90), the Mohammad Yunus Committee in 1988 (the foundation stone of Indian tourism), the National Action Plan in 1992, the National Strategy in 1996 and a separate Ministry of Tourism from 14 May 2000; the Incredible India campaign.
